paragraphs.text: That strange Bluetooth symbol hides two letters.
The emblem conceals two characters, formed by merging the runic symbols for H and B into a single shape.

The name pays tribute to King Harald Bluetooth, whose unification of Scandinavia inspired the goal of linking PCs and phones; Intel’s Jim Kardach proposed the mark as a temporary code name, intended to be replaced by RadioWire or PAN, with PAN already widespread and RadioWire’s trademark check expiring.

King Harald Bluetooth Gormsson, noted for uniting Denmark and Norway in 958, earned his nickname from a dead tooth of a dark blue‑grey colour. In 1996 Intel, Ericsson and Nokia convened to plan a short‑range radio standard. At that meeting Jim Kardich of Intel suggested Bluetooth as a temporary code name, inspired after he saw a picture of Harald Bluetooth’s runestone in a Viking history.
The practical problem was that PAN already had tens of thousands of hits on the internet, and a full trademark search on RadioWire could not be completed in time for launch.

The Bluetooth emblem is a bind rune merging the Younger Futhark characters for Harald’s initials, and its designer likened Harald’s historic unification of Scandinavia to the goal of linking computer and cellular ecosystems.
A symbol acts as an outward sign that conveys a sender’s message, enables layered communication, and its meaning is learned culturally rather than inherent.
Semiotics studies signs as communication, exploring signifier‑signified relations with visual and contextual cues; symbols can cause translation confusion when meanings differ across languages.
Symbols hold ideological, comparative, or isomorphic value; Tillich noted they are born and die, and a living symbol can reveal hidden meanings and point beyond itself to mysterious depths.

Symbol meanings evolve with culture or personal change, and context shifts interpretation; a symbolic action signals intent, and groups may use such actions to address criticism without direct change.

Bluetooth sounds like a technical acronym, but it is a king's nickname that was meant to be a placeholder. It was intended only as a placeholder name. The planned replacement names were RadioWire or PAN (Personal Area Networking).
A temporary code name became the permanent name and logo of a global wireless standard.
A symbol functions as a visual marker that conveys an idea, object, relationship, or formula.
The Bluetooth logo is a bind rune merging the Younger Futhark runes Hagall and Bjarkan, Harald's initials.
